Under challenge in this revision petition is the conviction and sentence rendered against the revision petitioner under Sections 420 and 471 of IPC.

2. The revision petitioner who is the first accused in Crime No.183 of 2005 of Rajapuram Police Station, stood trial before the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-I, Hosdurg in C.C.No.1733 of 2010 for committing the offences punishable under Sections 420, 468 and 471 of IPC.
3.

entities.text: Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-I, Hosdurg
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The prosecution case is that accused Nos.1 to 6 forged a cheque by misusing a cheque leaf issued by the ICICI Bank to one of its account holder, the second accused.
The first accused presented the said forged cheque before the Syndicate Bank, Chullikkara Branch through his account for payment.

It is alleged 2025:KER:74383 that the first accused dishonestly and fraudulently induced to credit the amount shown in the forged cheque into his personal account and the bank officials credited the amount in his account, without sending the cheque for collection to the drawee bank.

Immediately,
thereafter, the first accused withdrew Rs.34,000/- from his account by using a withdrawal slip.

Later, the Syndicate Bank came to know that the cheque thus presented by the first accused is a P.Razak @ Abdul Razak vs State Of Kerala on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/2754168/
2 forged one.
4.

sentences.text: The trial court, on an elaborate appreciation of evidence on record, found the first accused not guilty of committing an offence under Section 468 of IPC and acquitted him thereunder.
But it found the first accused guilty of committing the offences punishable under Sections 420 and 471 of IPC and convicted him thereunder.

It sentenced the first accused to undergo simple imprisonment for a period 2025:KER:74383 of six months under Section 471 of IPC and to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one year under Section 420 of IPC.
He was also ordered to pay compensation of Rs.34,000/- to the Syndicate Bank, Chullikkara Branch under Section 357(3) of Cr.P.C., with a default clause.
5. The first accused carried the matter in appeal by filing Crl.Appeal No.164 of 2015 before the Additional Sessions Court-II, Kasaragod.
The said court, by judgment dated 21.01.2016 dismissed the appeal.

6. Heard Adv.M.Sasindran, the learned counsel for the revision petitioner and Adv.Ranjit George,
the learned Public Prosecutor.
Perused the copies of records made available by the learned counsel for the revision petitioner.

7. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner submitted that both the trial court and 2025:KER:74383 the appellate court have failed to consider the fact that there is no evidence to prove the commission of forgery by the revision petitioner and therefore, the conviction under Section 471 of IPC is not sustainable.

He also submitted that the evidence of PW1 and PW2 regarding identification of the accused is not at all believable and there is no evidence to show that it is the revision petitioner who has presented Ext.P1 cheque.
8. Per contra, the learned Public Prosecutor supported the impugned judgments and contended that there are no grounds to interfere with the same.

9. It is a settled law that this Court while considering a revision petition, will not re- appraise the evidence on record and it is only in cases where the judgment is perverse, interference will be made.
In the instant case, the evidence of 2025:KER:74383 PW1 shows that the accused has come to the bank with Ext.P1 cheque and has requested the same to be discounted, without sending it for collection.
He also deposed that he had honoured Ext.P1 cheque then and there and has credited the amount into the account of the first accused.
He further stated that Ext.P2 is the withdrawal slip used by the accused to withdraw the said sum.
His evidence reveals that later when Ext.P1 cheque was sent for collection to the ICICI Bank, Kanhangad Branch, it returned as per Ext.P3 memo and he understood that the cheque is forged.
On that basis, he lodged Ext.P5 complaint before the police.
PW1 further stated that he had verified the signature in the withdrawal slip with the specimen signature of the accused available in the bank before disbursing the money.
10. It is to be seen that the evidence of PW1 is well supported by the evidence of PW2, who was 2025:KER:74383 the cashier, at the relevant time.

His evidence shows that he has previous acquaintance with the accused who is a regular customer of the bank and that he has given P.Razak @ Abdul Razak vs State Of Kerala on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/2754168/
3 Rs.34,000/- to him on the basis of Ext.P2 withdrawal slip presented by him.

sentences.text:
Thus from the evidence of these witnesses, it can be seen that it is the accused who has presented Ext.P1 cheque before the bank and has induced the bank to clear the cheque without sending it for collection and thereafter,
has received the money as per Ext.P2.
In fact, Ext.P12 report from FSL also confirms the fact that Ext.P2 has been drawn by the accused himself.

11. Be that as it may, it is to be seen that the evidence of PW5, the Manager of ICICI Bank, Kannur Branch clearly shows that Ext.P1 relates to the account of one Abdulla and that the signature in the cheque and the seal used in it is not that of the account holder.

His evidence also shows that there is 2025:KER:74383 no account in ICICI Bank in the name of 'Gencies ICICI Personal Loans' and that in all cheques of personal loans, the signature of the authorised officer and the seal of the bank will be there.

It is to be seen that there is no substantial challenge to the evidence of PW5 and therefore,
from his evidence, it can be safely found that Ext.P1 cheque produced by the accused is a forged one.

At this juncture, I will also take note of the evidence of PW4, which shows that it is she, who had filled up Ext.P1 cheque, by typewriting the name of the payee (name of the accused), amount and date on the basis of a request made by 3 persons, whom she could not identify.
Further, there is no case for the accused that he is not having an account with the Syndicate Bank and that he had received the cheque bona fide and on the belief that it is genuine.
In these circumstances, it can be safely 2025:KER:74383 inferred that the accused, while presenting Ext.P1 before the bank, had the knowledge that it was a forged one.
Hence, I find that the trial court and the appellate court have not committed any error/illegality in appreciating the evidence and in arriving at a conclusion of guilt against the accused.
Considering the nature and gravity of the offences, the sentence imposed also cannot be stated as excessive or unjust.
Ergo, I find no merit in this revision petition and the same is accordingly dismissed.
